xref.title: Donnie Darko Soundtrack Production (2001)
xref.body: In 2001, San Diego musician Michael Andrews was contacted by director Richard Kelly to work on the movie *Donnie Darko*. Andrews, who loved "Mad World" as a kid, decided it would be perfect for the soundtrack but needed to adapt it. He stripped the song down to basics—piano, a mellotron, and a few other flourishes—partly for artistic reasons and partly due to budgetary constraints, as he couldn't afford many additional musicians. He also slowed the tempo by approximately 50%. "Andrew thought that Mad World would be perfect for the soundtrack."

xref.title: Accidental Sound Development
xref.body: In 1985, Margot began singing with her brothers Michael and Peter in their garage. They accidentally developed their distinctive down-tempo, almost whispery sound after neighbors called the police on one of their rehearsals for making too much noise, forcing them to tone down their volume. "They soon developed an interesting down tempo, almost whispery sound. And then sort of came about by accident because the neighbors called the cops on one of the rehearsals for making too much noise so they just kind of toned it down."

xref.title: CR-78 Modifications
xref.body: As Ultravox's Canadian drummer, Warren Cann was fascinated by rhythm and the new possibilities offered by the Roland CR-78. He experimented by opening the machine and modifying its voltage regulators to prevent tempo drift from its sensitive control knob and to create a fatter bass drum sound, which can be heard on Ultravox's *Vienna* album. "So Warren opened it up and started playing with voltage regulators. He jury rigged away to keep tempo tight, as well as a way to make the bass drum sound fatter."

xref.title: Covered by The Clash
xref.body: American singer Vince Taylor's old blues song was used as a warm-up piece by The Clash during the recording sessions for their 1979 album "London Calling." Producer Guy Stevens secretly recorded the band's take on it, which he then accepted despite the band's protests about its sloppiness and tempo. "The clash went into the studio in the summer of 1979 to record what would become the London Calling album, producer Guy Stevens had all four guys warm up with a cover of an old blues song by American singer Vince Taylor."

xref.title: Formation and Genre
xref.body: Moist formed in Vancouver and gained widespread popularity by aligning with the "Grunge Wave" of the 1990s, producing mid-tempo songs that were highly successful on radio. Their sound became a staple of the Canadian rock scene. "They were formed in Vancouver and rode the Grunge Wave with a series of mid-tempo songs that worked very well on the radio."

xref.title: Lyric and Tempo Evolution
xref.body: "Buddy Holly" underwent several changes during its production. Early demos contained rap slang that was later removed. The lyrics initially referred to Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire but eventually morphed into Mary Tyler Moore and Buddy Holly. Furthermore, the song's tempo was increased in the studio and further tweaked to a higher pace during the mastering process. "Instead of the lyrics referring to Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire, they morphed into Mary Tyler Moore and Buddy Holly."

xref.title: Origin and Defining Trip Hop
xref.body: Hailing from Bristol, UK, Portishead helped to define the "Trip Hop" sound in 1994. This genre is characterized as a form of down-tempo music subtly integrating elements of electronic and hip hop, along with dashes of funk, soul, jazz, samples, and various sonic experimentation. "In 1994 they helped define a sound that became known as Trip Hop."

xref.title: Unconventional Song Structures
xref.body: Franz Ferdinand is known for experimenting with tempo changes and unconventional song structures, a characteristic Alex Kapranos attributes to a desire for bravery and experimentation in their music. He noted that their approach to "Take Me Out," with its contrasting fast verses and slow choruses, arose from a need to make both sections work effectively while maintaining a strong emphasis on melody within an experimental framework. "I guess it's being brave enough to use an unconventional song structure, you know, a laylite, sort of being a little bit experimental."
